name_ru: Лао Цун Чжэн Шань Сяо Чжун
aliases: Tong Mu Guan Laocong Lapsang Souchong
processing: Withered, rolled, oxidised and dried as a Tongmu black tea; whether a given lot is smoked over pine depends on the maker, so ask or smell before buying.
harvest_season: Little is documented for this style specifically; as with other Tongmu black teas, expect a spring picking.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted strips, typical of a Tongmu black tea made from mature leaf rather than buds.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber to reddish orange, typical of Tongmu black teas.
appearance_wet: Soft reddish-brown leaves, usually whole leaf rather than bud.
taste_profile: Tongmu black teas lean sweet and rounded, with a longan-like sweetness; smoked lots add pine. Woody depth is what buyers look for from older bushes, but tasting notes for this style are mostly from sellers.

brewing.notes: Treat it like other whole-leaf Chinese black teas: short steeps in a gaiwan, and lengthen them once the sweetness starts to thin.

vintage_note: Usually sold by harvest year, like other Tongmu black teas, and best within a few years while stored dry and sealed. 'Laocong' is a seller's claim about the age of the bushes with no bush age you can check from the bag, so a named village and maker count for more than the word itself.
description:
This is a black tea from the Tongmu area of the Wuyi Mountains, sold on the promise that the leaf comes from old bushes (laocong). It is a recognised enough idea locally that the Tongmu village black tea contest has a category for old-bush black tea.

There is no published definition of how old a bush must be, and little is documented about how these lots are made differently. As with other Tongmu black teas, the leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, and pine smoke is a choice rather than a given.

Expect the sweet, rounded character of the area rather than a loud smoke. Brew it in short steeps and judge it on how long the sweetness lasts, since that is the real test of whether the higher price means anything.

The term is a selling word as much as a description. Ask which village it came from and which year, and compare it side by side with an ordinary Tongmu Lapsang Souchong from the same maker.
history: Little is documented about old-bush Tongmu tea as a separate style. It sits inside the much older Tongmu black tea tradition and appears today mainly as a market term and as a category, 'old-bush black tea', in the Tongmu village tea contest, whose sixth edition closed in October 2025.
